On X, the Nobel Peace Prize winner was brief, posting, "I'm here with you all."
Machado's return is a direct challenge to interim President Delce Rodriguez, who took
over the country after U.S. troops captured the former leader, Nicolas Maduro, in January.
The Trump administration has sidelined the very popular Machado, who has said elections
need to be held soon.
The U.S. insists the country must first stabilize before elections, declining repeatedly to
set a date.
Edmundo Gonzalez, who had run against Maduro and is widely believed to have won the presidency
in 2024, says he too will return.
Posting also on X, he said, "Our sovereign voice returns with Machado to quote, 'Lead
and guide this process.'"
Kerry Khan, NPR News, Brasilia.
With little over a week to go until the midterm elections, top Democrats and Republicans are
on the campaign trail, including former President Obama, who rallied for Democratic candidates
in Ohio and Michigan yesterday, making sharp comments about President Trump, blaming him
for rising prices.
"Interest rates are up, and then there's gas, $4 again, $5 again, diesel, over $6 in climate."
Congress says Trump continued his campaign rally schedule yesterday visiting Georgia
once again.
Today, he'll hold a rally in Michigan.
This as control of both chambers of Congress hangs in the balance.
Attorney General Todd Blanche is defending a Justice Department lawsuit that seeks to
block Alaska from automatically certifying its U.S. Senate results if Republican Senator
Dan Sullivan loses in next week's vote because of another candidate with the same name.
Dylan Marks reports the top Democrat in the Senate race is joining others in asking a
judge to toss the lawsuit.
The suit argues that a second candidate on the ballot, a retired schoolteacher named
Daniel J. Sullivan, could confuse voters in the incumbent's tight race against Democrat
candidate Mary Peltola.
Asked on CNN's State of the Union whether the lawsuit was setting the stage for President
Trump to challenge the results, Blanche said his department was not "laying any groundwork"
for the president to do that.
"The relief that we are seeking is not to not certify.
It's to not certify if the law is broken.
So if the law is broken, and that's for Alaskan and the Alaskan court system to determine."
Alaska's courts had already ruled the second Sullivan could remain on the ballot, and state
officials had listed the senator as "Dan S. Sullivan" with his party label and incumbent
status to help tell the two men apart.
For NPR News, I'm Dylan Marks.
And you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The Archdiocese of New York and lawyers for 1,300 people who say they've been sexually
abused by clergy have agreed to an $800 million legal settlement.
That's the second biggest involving a Catholic archdiocese in the U.S. following a 2024 settlement
of $880 million involving the Archdiocese of Los Angeles.
News survivor attorney Jeff Anderson tells the AP the settlement represents a powerful
moment in the pursuit of justice, one that will bring healing and reconciliation.
One of the most recognizable brands in the NFL is organizing, and Piers John Stolenes
reports the Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders are unionizing.
The newly formed Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Association and the Cowboys released a joint
statement officially recognizing the new union.
The franchise said they will collectively bargain with the new union, calling the cheerleaders
an esteemed part of the Cowboys organization.
The cheerleaders' quest for better pay was chronicled in a highly popular Netflix docu-series
about the group, and following its airing, members said they worked to secure a 400 percent
pay increase for the 2025-26 season.
For years, the Cowboys faced fair-wage lawsuits from members of the cheerleading squad that
were eventually settled out of court.
One in 2019 saw a doubling of pay to $400 a game.
John Stolenes, NPR News.
On Wall Street this week, all eyes will be on the Federal Reserve meeting and their decision
on whether to raise the benchmark interest rates again.
The Fed raised interest rates in September for the first time in more than three years.
